chunk_findings.detail:
The write-back is gated on `res.output` being truthy and is done *before* anything consumes it, but the docstring promises `log_to` "receives the whole output of the command (the integrator keeps it for a parked entry)".

Concrete failure: the very scenario this bug is about is a command that exits non-zero with *empty or whitespace-only combined output* — e.g. `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files exited 1` where the hook's failure text went to a place the capture missed (or the stage died before emitting anything, as with an OOM-killed hook, a `timeout_s` expiry, or a wrapper that prints only to a tty). Then `res.output` is `""`, the `if` is skipped, **no file is created at `log_to`**, and the integrator's "keeps the ci log" contract silently degrades to "no log path at all" — the exact 15-minute-rerun-by-hand situation B539ec3de5a was filed to eliminate. The caller has no way to distinguish "log was empty" from "log was never written". Writing the file unconditionally (even for empty output, and even when `1`/`2` is returned) removes the ambiguity; at minimum the caller needs a documented guarantee about which of these two happened.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/cirun.py:76 (`log_to` write-back in `ci_run`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`log_to.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` plus `fsio.atomic_write` run *inside* `ci_run` unconditionally, with no guard on `res` being a usable result.

Concrete failure: `CI.run` returns an outcome whose `output` may be capped/truncated (the docstring says "the whole output"), and if the CI result ever reports output that is large (a full `--all-files` hook run on a big tree) this writes the entire capture blob to disk from the API layer for *every* caller that passes `log_to`, including successful runs, with no size bound and no rotation. The parked-entry case is the rare one; the success case is the common one, so a busy queue now accumulates one full-sized log file per run under `<run dir>`. That is a disk-growth defect introduced by the placement, not by the intent. I am flagging the unbounded/always-write aspect specifically because the change's stated purpose is to keep logs only for a *parked* entry.

I am not reporting the `fsync=False` choice itself, the `mkdir` race, or anything about the missing hunks, since I cannot demonstrate a failure for those from what is shown.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/cirun.py:89 (`fsio.atomic_write(log_to, res.output, fsync=False)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `assert isinstance(log, Path)` can never fail and therefore verifies nothing. `log` is bound on line 44 as `log = proj / parked["log"]`; the `proj` fixture is a `pathlib.Path`, and `Path.__truediv__` always returns a `Path` (the `os.PathLike` ABC guarantees this), so the expression is unconditionally `True` for every possible value of `parked["log"]`. If the intent was to validate the type/format of the `log` field coming out of `queue status` JSON, the check is on the wrong object (it inspects the locally-constructed `Path`, not `parked["log"]`, which is a `str` by the point of the earlier `in text` assertion). If the intent was to validate that the path is usable, the preceding `log.is_file()` and `log.read_text()` already do that, and would raise on a non-path. As written this line is dead weight that can mask a reviewer's impression that the log field's type is covered; removing it changes no test outcome.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_merge_queue_ci_log.py:49

chunk_findings.detail: The whole point of the change is that a parked item must have a CI log at the caller-supplied `log_to` path (the intent explicitly calls out "No failing hook, test id or log path in queue status or `.ddflow/runs/<item>/`"). The write is guarded by `and res.output`, so when the CI command fails without producing any captured output, no file is created at `log_to` and the parked entry again has no log. This is reachable: a pre-push hook that is killed by a signal, a hook that exits non-zero after writing only to a closed fd, or `CI.run(..., timeout_s=...)` timing out (code 2) all yield `res.output == ""` while `log_to` was requested — the caller then either names a path that does not exist or reports "no log", which is exactly the bug B539ec3de5a describes. Writing unconditionally (empty file included) would preserve the guarantee; the truthiness check silently drops it.

chunk_findings.detail:
The failing-test ids are read from a key the ci result does not carry. The same diff shows the ci result's own field for this data in `ddflow/services/ci.py`:

```python
#: failing test ids (and their reasons / failure tails) read from ALL of the output
failures: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
```

i.e. the ci outcome exposes test ids as the *keys* of `failures` (a dict id -> reason/tail), not as a `failed_tests` list. `_ci_detail` reads `d.get("output_tail")` from the same `out.data` dict (a real field of that result), so `d` is the result's data mapping; `d.get("failed_tests", [])` therefore silently returns `[]` and the test-id half of the fix is a no-op. Concretely, for the very scenario in the bug report — `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files` failing because of `tests/test_readme_catchup.py` — `names` gets the failing hook from `checks` but never the failing test id from `failures`, so the queue status still does not name the test that had to be discovered by re-running the stage (the stated 15-minute cost). Iterating `d.get("failures", {})` (or `list(...)`) is what names it.

chunk_findings.detail: The condition `if log_to is not None and not res.ok:` silently drops the log for every *successful* run, not just for the empty-output failure this bug is about. Previously `if log_to is not None and res.output:` wrote a log whenever the run produced output, pass or fail. Concretely: `ddflow ci run --log out.txt -- <cmd>` where `<cmd>` succeeds and prints anything (the normal case — pre-commit/hook output is verbose) now leaves `out.txt` non-existent, and any caller that records/report the requested log path (the same `_entry`/gate machinery the fix relies on) has a dangling reference guarded only by `log.exists()`. The change needed for the bug is "write the log even when `res.output` is empty on failure", i.e. dropping the `res.output` test; switching to `not res.ok` additionally removes success logs. The new test only asserts the silent-pass case (`SILENT` prints nothing), so it does not exercise — and does not justify — dropping the log for a passing run that *does* produce output.

chunk_findings.detail: The hunk removes `from pathlib import Path` from inside the `NOISY` script string while the script's final statement is still `sys.exit(1 if any("BAD" in p.read_text() for p in Path("knobs").glob("*.txt")) else 0)`. `NOISY` is written to `proj/check.py` and executed, so the script now raises `NameError: name 'Path' is not defined` before reaching `sys.exit`, unconditionally failing regardless of what is in `knobs/*.txt` — the conditional exit path the fixture is supposed to model is no longer exercised (note `SILENT`, added in the same hunk, *does* keep its `import`). Worse, the traceback appended to the captured output (`Traceback...`, the `File ".../check.py"` line, the source line, the `^^^^` caret and `NameError: ...`, i.e. ~5-6 lines after the printed `E501 the very last line of the output`) pushes that line further from the end, so the assertion `"very last line" in row["tail"]` depends on `TAIL_LINES` being larger than the traceback and can fail on any interpreter that emits a slightly longer traceback.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change removes `from pathlib import Path` from inside the `NOISY` script body, but that script still references `Path` in its last statement:

```python
sys.exit(1 if any("BAD" in p.read_text() for p in Path("knobs").glob("*.txt")) else 0)
```

The string is written to `check.py` and executed by the merge queue (which is exactly why the sibling `SILENT` fixture carries its own `from pathlib import Path`). With the import gone, the intended exit-code logic is dead code: executing the script raises `NameError: name 'Path' is not defined` before `any(...)`/`sys.exit(...)` is ever evaluated, so the check exits 1 via an unhandled exception rather than via the knobs check, and a `NameError` traceback is appended after the `E501 the very last line of the output` line. Consequences: (a) any `NOISY`-based case that relies on the script exiting 0 when no `knobs/*.txt` contains `BAD` can no longer do so; (b) the assertions `"very last line" in row["tail"]` / `... in text` now depend on the appended traceback being shorter than `TAIL_LINES` — if the tail window is small, the traceback displaces "very last line" and the test fails, independent of the production change. The fixture should keep the `from pathlib import Path` line inside the string.

chunk_findings.detail: The stub previously interpreted the `slow` file's **content** as a duration: `if slow.exists(): time.sleep(float(slow.read_text() or 2))` — i.e. "hold CI for N seconds", with an empty file meaning the 2 s default. The new stub interprets **existence** as an unbounded hold: `while hold.exists() and time.time() < deadline: time.sleep(0.05)`, with `deadline = time.time() + 120`. Only `test_two_integrators_do_not_run_at_once` was updated to `hold.unlink(missing_ok=True)`; every other caller of this shared fixture that writes/`touch`es `proj.parent / "slow"` to make CI take a bounded time (the file's old, documented meaning) and never deletes it will now have its CI loop for the full 120 s instead of sleeping the requested duration — and if the integrator enforces its own CI gate/timeout (the very thing the bug description references), that CI is killed and the test fails rather than merely running slow. Concretely: a test that does `slow.write_text("1")` and expects CI to take 1 s now blocks ~120 s, and a test that relies on the old `or 2` empty‑file default now blocks ~120 s. The regression test should not require changing the meaning of a shared helper; either keep the content‑as‑duration behavior for callers that don't unlink the file (e.g. fall back to a content‑driven sleep when present), or update/lock down every caller of `slow`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new expression guarantees a positive ETA only when `ahead > 0`; it does not implement the invariant it advertises in the adjacent comment ("work not done has an ETA of at least a second") nor the one in the new test's docstring ("An ETA for unfinished work never reads 0"). `ahead` is the mean duration of the last merged entries, and a merge can legitimately be recorded with a duration of exactly `0.0` — e.g. a no-op / already-up-to-date / fast-forward merge, or any merge whose `started_at` and `finished_at` come from the same timestamp value on a coarse clock. In that case `typical_s(...) == 0.0`, so for the queued `T2`/`T3` the code executes `ahead += 0.0` and `math.ceil(0.0) == 0`, and `queue status` prints `eta 0s` for work that has not run — the exact symptom of Ba176075b5f. The same holds for any `ahead <= 0` (e.g. an entry that has already been running longer than the typical duration, which makes the accumulated `ahead` non-positive), where `math.ceil` returns `0` or a negative number of seconds rather than raising the estimate to 1. The fix should clamp, e.g. `row["eta_s"] = max(1, math.ceil(ahead))` (or a documented negative guard), and the regression test should parametrize `took` with `0.0` — the boundary case of the very bug being fixed — not just `[0.2, 0.01, 0.5]`.
